In early stage (stages I and II) non-small cell lung carcinomas (NSCLC), surgical resection remains the therapy of choice. However, almost 40–55% of these tumours recur following surgery (Ambrogi et al., 2011). The clinical care of lung cancer patients would substantially benefit from accurate prognostic evaluation. Currently, TNM staging system of lung cancer based on the anatomic extent of disease is well recognised and widely adopted, which allows tumours of comparable anatomic extent to be grouped together (Goldstraw et al., 2016). Staging guides treatment and provides a broad prediction of prognosis, however individual characteristics, histology, and/or therapy characteristics may impact survival results, as seen by variation within stage groups. In the refinement of the staging system, non-anatomical predictors such as gene mutations and biomarker profiles were proposed to be incorporated (Giroux et al., 2018). However, the gene profiling approach relies on tissue sampling, and in addition, may not fully explain the intratumoural heterogeneity seen in NSCLC. Besides, such tests have barriers in deploying to routine oncology workflows due to high turnaround time, complexity, and cost (Malone et al., 2020). To predict the patient's prognosis and to optimise individual clinical management, prognostic predictors such as TNM system and imaging-based high throughput quantitative biomarkers, radiomics, have been widely used to describe tumours (Du et al., 2019; Aonpong et al., 2020; Bera et al., 2022; Carmody et al., 1980; Chirra et al., 2019; Mirsadraee et al., 2012; van Griethuysen et al., 2017). Artificial intelligence (AI) methods, especially some deep learning (DL) models, have recently been regarded as potentially valuable tools (Chilamkurthy et al., 2018; Nabulsi et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2019). DL models generated multiple quantitative assessments for tumour characteristics, which have the potential to describe tumour phenotypes with more predictive power than the clinical model (Xu et al., 2019). While the anatomical structures in a medical image are functionally and mechanically related, most AI-based methods do not take these interdependencies and relationships into account. This leads to instability and poor generalisation of performance (Zhou et al., 2021). With recent advancements in AI technology, several novel models have been proposed. Notably, the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) model permits exceptional capabilities in natural language processing fields such as language translation and was later applied to the computer vision field and outperformed all state-of-the-art models given large amounts of training data (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020). This provides an intuitive reason to apply the Transformer model to the medical image to generate additional meaning for tumour features, as images were processed in sequence with inherent interdependencies (Zhou et al., 2022). The majority of current prognostic prediction methods have focused mainly either specific to their own domains, such as focusing solely on imaging data, whereas in clinical practice non-imaging clinical data such as sex, age, and disease history all play critical roles in disease prognosis prediction (Holzinger et al., 2019). Although some researchers have used multi-modal techniques (Xue et al., 2018) to combine that information, it is not easy to explain how the various types of data interacted and how they contributed to the final prediction. Due to their lack of explanatory power, those models may not be easily applied in clinical practice (London, 2019). Another type of neural network, called a graph neural network (GNN) (Kipf and Welling, 2016), which deals with data that has a graph structure, enables researchers to create more flexible ways to embed various types of data. For example, nodes and edges in a graph might represent a variety of different types of data (imaging and clinical demographics information), and analysing these entities reveals the role of various data sources. In this study, we proposed a GNN-based model that leverages imaging and non-imaging data for the prediction of the survival of patients with early stage NSCLC. Patients were represented as a population graph, whereby each patient corresponded to a graph node and was associated with a tumour feature vector that was learnt from the Transformer model, and graph edge weights between patients were derived from a similarity score that was derived from phenotypic data, such as demographics, tumour location, cancer type, and TNM staging. This population graph was used to train a GraphSAGE (Hamilton et al., 2017) model for classifying individual patient's risk of overall survival (OS) and recurrence. Additionally, we attempted to determine the relative importance of imaging and non-imaging features within this model. The proposed model was trained and tested on a large data set, followed by external validation using a publicly available data set. Methods Participants The study included consecutive patients who received surgery for early stage NSCLC between January 2011 and December 2013 who matched the criteria. Inclusion criteria included: (1) pathologically proven stage I or stage II NSCLC; (2) preoperative thin-section CT image data; and (3) complete follow-up survival data. Patients undergoing neoadjuvant therapy were excluded from the study. This retrospective study protocol was approved by the Shanghai Pulmonary Hospital's Institutional Review Board (ref: L21-022-2) and informed consent was waived owing to retrospective nature. Additionally, patients who met our criteria were retrieved from the NSCLC Radiogenomics (Bakr et al., 2018) data set as an external validation set (see Figure 1 for the internal and external inclusion criteria flowchart). Figure 1 Download asset Open asset Overall flow of the study in both internal and external data set. We only used patients' initial CT scans in this study. For the main cohort, all CT scans were acquired using Somatom Definition AS+ (Siemens Medical Systems, Germany) and iCT256 (Siemens Medical Systems, Germany; Philips Medical Systems, Netherlands). All image data were rebuilt using a 1-mm slice thickness and a 512×512 mm2 matrix. Intravenous contrast was administered in accordance with institutional clinical practice. Clinical data in this study were manually collected from medical records and were anonymised. Outpatient records and telephone interviews were used to collect follow-up data. The period between the date of surgery and the date of death or the final follow-up was defined as OS. Recurrence-free survival (RFS) was calculated from the date of surgery to the date of recurrence, death, or last follow-up. (More details about internal scan parameters and follow-up strategies can be found in Appendix 1). Image annotation and pre-processing Patients' tumour region was manually labelled by experienced radiologists using 3D Slicer (Fedorov et al., 2012), with a centre seed point defining a bounding box. The regions of interest (ROIs) were first annotated by two junior thoracic surgeons (Y.S. and J.D. with 5 and 3 years of experience, respectively), then the consensus on ROI was obtained by a discussion with a senior radiologist (with more than 25 years of experience). For image pre-processing, we first normalised all CT images and removed the surrounding noises such as bones by manual thresholding. The size of all tumour segments was fixed to 128×128×64 mm3. Small tumours were zero-padded. To reduce the computational cost, we resized the padded segments into 64×64×36 mm3 and subsequently resized them as 2D square images (each row contained six tumour slices) with the size of 384×384 mm2 as shown in Figure 2A. Figure 2 Download asset Open asset Tumour image processing and feature generation. (A) Tumour images normalisation, reshaping, and padding to standard sizes, then re-arranged into 2D images. (B) Generating 1D Transformer survival features from pretrained Transformer model. Tumour Transformer feature generator When pretrained on a large data set and transferred to image recognition benchmarks, it has been shown that Vision Transformer (ViT) can achieve excellent results while requiring significantly less computational resources to train than state-of-the-art convolutional models (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020). To this end, we reasoned that by replacing the traditional CNN feature generator architecture with a Transformer structure could be an approach to produce meaningful survival-relevant features. In this study, we used a ViT pretrained on a large-scale data set (ImageNet-21k; Ridnik et al., 2021) as the feature generator, which takes 2D tumour segments as inputs. To meet the standard requirements of the sequence model, the input images were divided into 36 ordered patches and position embedding in the first step, followed by a linear projection function before entering the Transformer Encoder. We replaced the original classification layer with a fully connected layer to generate a 1D feature vector. The detailed implementation is illustrated in Figure 2B. The 1D feature vector was then assigned as the node feature for the individual patient in the graph network. Patient survival graph network A population graph method was used to leverage imaging and non-imaging data. Each patient was regarded as a node in a graph and its edge with neighbour was derived from a similarity score which was determined by the product between four component scores, namely demographics (gender and age), tumour location, cancer type (histology), and TNM staging (for more detail, refer to the Appendix 1 for a detailed explanation of similarity scores). Two patients would be connected to each other if they shared similar component scores. The features of an individual patient (node feature) were obtained from the Transformer Encoder trained on the tumour images mentioned above. Graph-based neural network structure We applied a graph-based deep neural network structure called GraphSAGE in this study. The proposed network took the whole population graph, along with the edge and node features as the input and generated a risk score in the last layer for each patient node as the output (see Figure 3). Within the network, every node feature was updated by an aggregation of information from its neighbours and itself, while the importance of different neighbours varied by the corresponding edges' weight. Figure 3 Download asset Open asset Population graph building and model prediction pipeline. (A) Each patient was regarded as a node and the Transformer-generated feature was regarded as node features. (B) Graph edges and the relevant weights were defined by their similarity scores. (C) We then put the whole population graph to train the GraphSAGE network in order to make a prediction for each patient (pink indicates high risk and blue indicates low risk). (D) Node updating inside the GraphSAGE network. We applied a two-layer GraphSAGE and global meaning pooling structure, aiming to allow each patient's information to be updated, first from its second neighbours and then its neighbours and itself consequentially. In order to emphasise the target of survival prediction, we specifically replaced the cross-entropy loss with Cox proportional hazards loss function (Katzman et al., 2018) which both considered the survival time and events when training the network. The proposed network was implemented in Python, using the Deep Graph Library with Pytorch backend. Statistics analysis All patients from the main data set were randomly separated into training, validation, and testing sets with the proportion of 75%, 12.5%, and 12.5% separately. We also tested the model on the external validation data set. The proposed model was compared with the TNM staging system which was generally used in clinical practice and a ResNet-Graph model which has the same graph structure (using clinical features to define the similarity score) as our proposed model while the node feature was generated by a pretrained ResNet-18 model (Khanna et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2019) (using imaging features). To evaluate whether there were statistically significant variations in survival between positive and negative groups, the area under the receiver operator characteristic curve (AUC) was determined for OS and RFS prediction to compare the models' performance. The Kaplan–Meier (KM) method was used to generate prognostic and survival estimates for groups with low and high risk (both for OS and RFS), which were stratified according to the training set's median prediction probability, with the log-rank test employed to establish statistical significance. To quantify the net benefits of survival prediction, we quantified the net reclassification improvement (NRI) and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), as well as performed a decision curve analysis (DCA). All of the analyses above were performed in Python using the Lifelines package. An additional subanalysis was performed on the test data set to explore the relationship between patients' clinical information and imaging features contributing to risk prediction. We generated a sub-graph visualisation using PyVis and a KM analysis was used for several sub-graphs to evaluate our model's ability to separate high-risk patients. Finally, as a proof of concept, we plotted two patients' nodes feature changes before and after one layer processing using a correlation heatmap, along with its neighbours' edge weights analysis to try to understand the inner workings of our model. Results Data description In the main cohort, we initially enrolled 2309 patients and after exclusion based on our criteria, a total of 1705 NSCLC patients were included in the study. The median age was 61 (interquartile range, 55–66 years). There were 1010 males (59.2%) and 695 women (40.8%). Tumours were more frequently located in the upper lobes (1018, 59.7%). A total of 1235 patients (72.4%) had adenocarcinoma, while 391 patients (22.9%) had squamous cell carcinoma. The distribution of pathologic stages was as follows: stage IA was present in 791 patients (46.4%), stage IB was present in 607 patients (35.6%), stage IIA was present in 133 patients (7.8%), and stage IIB was present in 174 patients (10.2%). The OS and RFS rates were 78·2% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 76.2–80.2%) and 74.2% (70.8–77.6%), respectively. The external validation data set included a total of 127 patients of which 32 (25.2%) were females and 95 (74.8%) males, with a median age of 69 (interquartile range, 46–87 years). Upper lobe tumours were also more prevalent (76 patients, 59.8%). Among them 95 patients were diagnosed with adenocarcinoma and 30 with squamous cell carcinoma. Methods: The study included 1705 patients with lung cancer (stages I and II), and a public data set for external validation (n=127). We proposed a graph with edges representing non-imaging patient characteristics and nodes representing imaging tumour region characteristics generated by a pretrained Vision Transformer. The model was compared with a TNM model and a ResNet-Graph model. To evaluate the models' performance, the area under the receiver operator characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) was calculated for both OS and RFS prediction. The Kaplan–Meier method was used to generate prognostic and survival estimates for low- and high-risk groups, along with net reclassification improvement (NRI), integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), and decision curve analysis. An additional subanalysis was conducted to examine the relationship between clinical data and imaging features associated with risk prediction. Results: Our model achieved AUC values of 0.785 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.716–0.855) and 0.695 (95% CI: 0.603–0.787) on the testing and external data sets for OS prediction, and 0.726 (95% CI: 0.653–0.800) and 0.700 (95% CI: 0.615–0.785) for RFS prediction. Additional survival analyses indicated that our model outperformed the present TNM and ResNet-Graph models in terms of net benefit for survival prediction. Conclusions: Our Transformer-Graph model was effective at predicting survival in patients with early stage lung cancer, which was constructed using both imaging and non-imaging clinical features. Some high-risk patients were distinguishable by using a similarity score function defined by non-imaging characteristics such as age, gender, histology type, and tumour location, while Transformer-generated features demonstrated additional benefits for patients whose non-imaging characteristics were non-discriminatory for survival outcomes. Editor's evaluation This work constructed a population graph deep learning model using machine learning-generated imaging features and non-imaging clinical characteristics that were proven to be effective at predicting the survival of patients with early-stage NSCLC, which help us understand the imaging and non-imaging features in determining NSCLC populations with a high risk of recurrence, and the high predictive accuracy proves its novelty and significance. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.80547.sa0 Decision letter Reviews on Sciety eLife's review process Introduction Lung cancer is expected to account for more than 1.80 million deaths worldwide in 2021, making it the top cause of cancer-related mortality (Siegel et al., 2021). In early stage (stages I and II) non-small cell lung carcinomas (NSCLC), surgical resection remains the therapy of choice. However, almost 40–55% of these tumours recur following surgery (Ambrogi et al., 2011). The clinical care of lung cancer patients would substantially benefit from accurate prognostic evaluation. Currently, TNM staging system of lung cancer based on the anatomic extent of disease is well recognised and widely adopted, which allows tumours of comparable anatomic extent to be grouped together (Goldstraw et al., 2016). Staging guides treatment and provides a broad prediction of prognosis, however individual characteristics, histology, and/or therapy characteristics may impact survival results, as seen by variation within stage groups. In the refinement of the staging system, non-anatomical predictors such as gene mutations and biomarker profiles were proposed to be incorporated (Giroux et al., 2018). However, the gene profiling approach relies on tissue sampling, and in addition, may not fully explain the intratumoural heterogeneity seen in NSCLC. Besides, such tests have barriers in deploying to routine oncology workflows due to high turnaround time, complexity, and cost (Malone et al., 2020). To predict the patient's prognosis and to optimise individual clinical management, prognostic predictors such as TNM system and imaging-based high throughput quantitative biomarkers, radiomics, have been widely used to describe tumours (Du et al., 2019; Aonpong et al., 2020; Bera et al., 2022; Carmody et al., 1980; Chirra et al., 2019; Mirsadraee et al., 2012; van Griethuysen et al., 2017). Artificial intelligence (AI) methods, especially some deep learning (DL) models, have recently been regarded as potentially valuable tools (Chilamkurthy et al., 2018; Nabulsi et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2019). DL models generated multiple quantitative assessments for tumour characteristics, which have the potential to describe tumour phenotypes with more predictive power than the clinical model (Xu et al., 2019). While the anatomical structures in a medical image are functionally and mechanically related, most AI-based methods do not take these interdependencies and relationships into account. This leads to instability and poor generalisation of performance (Zhou et al., 2021). With recent advancements in AI technology, several novel models have been proposed. Notably, the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) model permits exceptional capabilities in natural language processing fields such as language translation and was later applied to the computer vision field and outperformed all state-of-the-art models given large amounts of training data (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020). This provides an intuitive reason to apply the Transformer model to the medical image to generate additional meaning for tumour features, as images were processed in sequence with inherent interdependencies (Zhou et al., 2022). The majority of current prognostic prediction methods have focused mainly either specific to their own domains, such as focusing solely on imaging data, whereas in clinical practice non-imaging clinical data such as sex, age, and disease history all play critical roles in disease prognosis prediction (Holzinger et al., 2019). titulo: The Return of Intentional Forest Fires
resumen: On 11 October 2021—Indigenous Peoples’ Day—Frank Lake took his children to visit a prescribed burn above the Klamath River, in remote northwest California. The flames crept along low to the ground, devouring thick growths of invasive Himalaya berry, clearing fallen wood from the forest floor. “I wanted my kids to be around that fire and see that this is what our community does,” says Lake. A member of the Karuk Tribe and a research ecologist with the US Forest Service (USFS) Pacific Southwest Research Station, Lake has spent much of his career studying the impact of fire suppression on ancestral Karuk land—and working to restore the ecosystem with intentional fire. The 12-acre burn in a patch of forest dubbed the Patterson Unit was one small step toward that goal. Indigenous burning traditions, like those of the Karuk, once shaped the landscapes of the western United States. Many ecologists believe that learning from such traditions is vital to address the ongoing Western wildland fire crisis, in which uncontrollable blazes scorch increasingly large swaths of land. Lake collaborated with ecologist Susan Prichard of the University of Washington and more than 30 other scientists on a trio of articles, published in Ecological Applications in 2021, that laid out the supporting evidence and rationale for an urgent shift in the way fire is managed in the West. “Despite calls to restore fire as a cultural and ecological process,” they wrote, “the dominant approach is aggressive suppression.… An intentional merging of Indigenous and Western knowledge is needed to restore active fire regimes to western North American forests.” Before the arrival of White colonists during the California Gold Rush, the Karuk and their neighbors, the Hupa and Yurok, set frequent fires in the rugged Klamath Mountains. They burned to keep prairies open, to stop Douglas-fir from growing up and shading out oaks, and to control the numbers of weevils infesting the acorn crop, a staple food. They burned to trigger fresh growth of hazel, a shrub whose young, flexible shoots are needed to weave the baskets native people use for gathering and cooking food and for carrying babies. Recognizing when and where to set a fire was part of native culture, passed down from one generation to the next. In 1911, an act of Congress established the USFS. The agency's founding mission was to suppress every wildfire, on the theory that this would produce the maximum amount of harvestable timber. Indigenous burning was outlawed, and native people were forced to fight the fires that they saw as essential to caring for their land. “Indigenous people were told, “You either go suppress fires, or you're gonna be thrown in jail,”” says Lake. Ninety-eight percent of ancestral Karuk land is now controlled by the Six Rivers and Klamath National Forests. Decades of USFS management have transformed the forests. Instead of open, mixed-species woodlands that included oaks and other hardwoods, the mountains are blanketed with dense stands of Douglas-fir—a very flammable kind of forest. The USFS built a machinery of fire suppression that became all too successful. Over time, forests filled in with tightly packed trees, while fallen leaves and branches accumulated on the ground. The USFS and other agencies still succeed in stifling 98% of wildfires, but the remaining 2% ignite and keep burning when the air is hot, fuels are dry, and the wind pushes flames through the forest. The size and severity of wildfires has increased steadily in the western United States since the 1980s, as forests overloaded with fuel burn in extreme fire weather, made more common and more intense by global warming. The Karuk homeland has experienced a series of such fires. The King Titus fire of 1987 burned 60,000 acres, the 2008 Mill fire 66,000. In 2014, the Happy Camp Complex fire burned more than 132,000 acres, destroying eight buildings. The Slater Fire of 2020 killed two people and burned 197 homes in the town of Happy Camp, the seat of Karuk tribal government, and blazed across more than 157,000 acres. In 2021, the McCash fire burned close to 95,000 acres, threatened the surviving buildings in Happy Camp, and made the air in Orleans, where many Karuk people live, dangerous to breathe. Karuk country is a microcosm of the fire management crisis plaguing the West. In studies of fire-scarred trees, Alan Taylor, a professor of geography and ecology at Pennsylvania State University, found that before European settlement, fire in the Klamath Mountains was far more common than he had expected. “The implication of that high fire frequency was that fuels never tended to accumulate very much,” says Taylor. “Fire could easily be stopped by small barriers, ridge tops, rock outcrops.” So fires in the time of Native American management recurred often—every few years—and stayed small, about 260 acres. In a study of recent wildfires in the region, Taylor found that the large fires of recent years have been burning intensely, transforming the vegetation in ways that leave the land more vulnerable to repeated severe fires. The Karuk survived the genocidal attacks of gold miners, soldiers, and vigilantes. They never ceded their land and, regardless of who owns it on paper, see themselves as its caretakers. They have held tenaciously to their culture of fire. “All Karuk families have stories of an auntie or a grandmother going to jail for burning,” says Craig Tucker, a natural resource policy consultant for the tribe. “She'd burn a patch so that the hazel sticks would come back healthy the next year, so she can make her baskets. They persisted; they were determined to keep their traditions alive.” A strong body of scientific evidence supports the need for fuels reduction and intentional fire in the Klamath Mountains and throughout the West. “There's been a tremendous jump in tree densities that coincides with the exclusion of fire,” says Eric Knapp, a research ecologist with the USFS Pacific Southwest Research Station. The pattern can easily be seen by comparing historical photographs of open forests pocked with recently burned patches to present-day photos of the same places, now blanketed with trees. Knapp has studied altered fire ecology in both the Klamath Mountains and the Sierra Nevada. In 2008, he revisited 40 acres of Sierra Nevada forest where, in 1929, early USFS scientists had mapped every tree. The site had not burned since 1889, and Knapp found the number of trees growing there had more than doubled. “One key thing that popped up,” he says, “is there are very few gaps. It used to be that the forest was composed of groups of trees that were intermixed with gaps.” When a fire came through, even if it climbed into the canopy of one clump of trees, killing them, it would soon die out, unable to jump the gap to the next clump. “By infilling, and creating fuel continuity across the forest, we've completely changed the way fire behaves,” explains Knapp. Fire suppression has set the stage for infernos that burn across hundreds of thousands of acres. Today's megafires not only burn much larger areas, but they burn more intensely than most fires did in the era of Native American management. A blaze that burns hot enough to kill off a whole group of trees is called a stand-replacing fire, and although such fires occurred before settlement, they were relatively rare and small. A pair of early USFS scientists who argued for the policy of fire suppression pointed to examples of stand-replacing fire, appalled at a 90-acre area where every tree had died. Today, stand-replacing fires occur on a mind-blowing scale. During the 2021 Dixie Fire, which burned more than 963,000 acres in Northern California and wiped out the town of Greenville, “a 32,000 acre patch burned, and there's no live tree left in it,” says Knapp. “That's just unprecedented.” Knapp points out that the blackened land left behind by recent large fires can serve as anchor points for future intentional burns. “We know from experience that if an area in the Klamath Mountains burned within the last 5 years, it's probably not going to carry fire,” he says. “So you could burn with a lot less risk, take advantage of that patchwork [of recent burns] to start chewing up some of that excess fuel. We would have to be more nimble in our planning and think at bigger scales. It would be an entirely different way of thinking about how to get out of this problem.” To keep prescribed fires from burning too hot, workers at the Patterson Unit and many other burns cut some of the smaller trees in the area before the fire is lit. In Karuk country, cut trees and shrubs are most often piled along roadsides and burned during late fall or winter. In some other cases, thinning may involve commercial cutting of trees large enough to be bound for a lumber mill. A number of studies have shown that a combination of thinning and intentional fire are needed to restore forests altered by decades of fire suppression. “In places where fire has been excluded for decades, you can't just go out and burn the way the Karuk did it 2000 years ago,” says Tucker. “We're trying to get back to real traditional Karuk fires, to use those traditional methods, but it's going to take some chainsaws, and maybe some bulldozers, to get there.” The need to mechanically remove trees upsets some conservationists, who distrust any kind of logging. After decades of clear-cut logging on USFS land, protests led to a shift in policy formulated under the Northwest Forest Plan of 1994. Concern for the survival of the northern spotted owl, a threatened species associated with old-growth forests, fueled demands for change. Under the plan, older forests were protected from disturbance while fire suppression continued. In a recent review, USFS researchers found that older forests grown thick with fuels have experienced larger patches of high-intensity fire, destroying habitat for the northern spotted owl. Fire is an integral part of the ecosystem, which must be restored to keep the forest healthy. “In terms of encouraging more prescribed burning, we've got an uphill challenge,” says Prichard. “But the public is starting to understand that we need to kind of get immunized, take a little vaccination in prescribed burning in order to prevent the big wildfires. Social acceptance is huge, because a lot of the big restoration projects get delayed in a kind of paralysis by analysis. If there's more social acceptance to use of prescribed burning, then a lot of projects can finally move forward and not be so contested.” Although many USFS researchers are involved in studying fire history and fuels reduction, the agency has been slow to act on their findings. Over the past 30 years, the USFS has become more dedicated to fighting fire than ever. In 1995, toward the end of the long logging boom in Western forests, fire suppression accounted for about 16% of the agency's budget. Soon after, the amount of money the USFS invested in stopping wildfires began to skyrocket. In recent years, suppression has taken up about half the agency's funding. In 2021, out of a total budget of $5.3 billion, $2.4 billion was designated for fire suppression. About $10 million was earmarked for work to improve forest conditions, which would include prescribed burning. It is difficult to track how much of that money was actually spent on fuels reduction or prescribed fire, because, in years of intense megafires, money is often diverted from such projects to fund firefighting. The relationship between the USFS and the Karuk tribe has improved in some meaningful ways. Staff at the Six Rivers and Klamath National Forests collaborate with Lake and other tribal members to conduct prescribed burns aimed at triggering new growth of plants needed for basketry, including beargrass and hazel. The Western Klamath Restoration Partnership, known to locals as WKRP, brings together tribal and community members and some sympathetic USFS employees to conduct cultural and prescribed burns and helps to train people to do this work through a training exchange program called TREX. The Patterson burn, as well as a prescribed fire at the ancient Karuk ceremonial ground of Tishawnik and several other projects, was done in the fall of 2021 by tribal members and TREX participants. Still, these efforts need to be scaled up by orders of magnitude to address the problem. The USFS and other government agencies remain steeped in a culture that often dismisses Indigenous knowledge and reflexively seeks to stomp out fire. “Most people today view fire through a lens of fear,” says Bill Tripp, a Karuk tribal member and director of the tribe's Department of Natural Resources. “A lot of people look at fire as something that's inherently bad. Karuk people view fire as more of a relation. [We] view everything as having a spirit of its own and a purpose in the place where it is. Fire has always been a very active component of our ecosystem. To survive in the western Klamath Mountains without fire engines and steel hand tools, in a culture that lives in permanent wooden houses, you're gonna have to have a very intimate relationship with fire.” Tripp was taught Karuk burning traditions by his great-grandmother. When he was 4 years old, she handed him a box of matches and set him the task of burning across 10 feet of ground covered in fallen leaves. “It was one of those cold late winter mornings,” he remembers. “The very top layer of those leaves were dry, but most of them were wet. You'd light a leaf on fire, half of it would burn, and it would go out.” Tripp discovered that if he rearranged the dry leaves, he could get the fire to carry. “I used all the matches, but I got it done. titulo: Fifth Consensus Guidelines for the Management of Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting: Executive Summary
resumen: Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is a common adverse event after surgery and anesthesia. Optimal management of PONV requires a multidisciplinary approach, with evidence-based care and appropriate institutional infrastructure.1 The Fifth Consensus Guidelines brought together an international, multidisciplinary panel of experts to review the available scientific literature to provide a comprehensive, evidence-based update on PONV management. This is the executive summary of the 5th PONV consensus guideline. The full guideline document is available as supplementary digital content (Supplemental Digital Content 1, appendix 1, https://links.lww.com/AA/F568). This iteration of the guideline provides updates on topics including PONV risk factors, risk reduction interventions, single antiemetic and combination options for PONV and postdischarge nausea and vomiting (PDNV), PONV management in children; pharmacoeconomics, PONV management within enhanced recovery pathways (ERP). The rationale for the updated PONV management algorithm will also be discussed. The current guidelines are prepared following the Cochrane Handbook for conducting the search, the PRISMA 2020 for reporting, and PRISMA-S extension for searches (SDC Supplemental Digital Content 1, appendix 1, https://links.lww.com/AA/F568 and Supplemental Digital Content 2, appendix 2, https://links.lww.com/AA/F569). The quality of evidence is graded using the system developed by the American Society of Anesthesiologists’ (ASA) acute pain management practice guideline,1 and was used in the previous PONV consensus guideline (SDC 3, appendix 3, https://links.lww.com/AA/F570). The gradings are highlighted in bold. GUIDELINE 1. IDENTIFY PATIENTS’ RISK FOR PONV PONV risk assessment tools and risk stratification protocols are effective in reducing PONV (B1).1 PONV risk scores can be used to inform and guide therapy, reducing institutional level PONV rates, using the Apfel simplified score (Figure 1A) for risk stratification.1,2 Patients without any Apfel risk factors should be considered low risk; those with 1 to 2 risk factors as medium risk; patients with ≥3 as high risk of PONV. Reminder systems increase adherence to a risk stratified management algorithm.3Figure 1.: A, Simplified risk score from Apfel et al to predict the patient’s risk for PONV. 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 risk factors correspond to PONV risks of approximately 10%, 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80%, respectively. B, Simplified risk score for PDNV in adults from Apfel et al to predict the risk for PDNV in adults. 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 risk factors correspond to PDNV risks of approximately 10%, 20%, 30%, 50%, 60%, and 80%, respectively. PDNV = post-discharge nausea and vomiting; PONV = postoperative nausea and vomiting; PACU = post-anesthesia care unit. Reproduced with permission from ASERP. For permission requests, contact [email protected].There is ongoing discussion on adopting a more liberal approach to PONV prophylaxis1 to address undetected risk factors, non-adherence to risk-stratified PONV algorithms and ambiguity in interpreting individual risk factors.4 This is supported by increased adoption of general multimodal PONV prophylaxis as part of enhanced recovery pathways.5 Increasing evidence supports the safety of antiemetics at perioperative dosages, this may shift the paradigm further towards liberal combination antiemetics.6 However, practice shifts towards general, multimodal prophylaxis does not discredit the validity of PONV prediction scores, nor an appropriately implemented risk-adapted PONV protocol. Novel PONV Risk Factors Literature since the last PONV consensus guideline reported several novel risk factors for PONV. A retrospective study of 160,000 patients identified a strong association between lower preoperative physical fitness (ASA classification 3) and decreased likelihood of developing PONV (SDC 3, Table S1, https://links.lww.com/AA/F570 B1).7 A smaller retrospective analysis demonstrated that higher hemoglobin and hematocrit (Hct) were associated with less PONV (B1),8 with Hct level >39.3% being optimal. Both elevated neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio and platelet/lymphocyte ratio were associated with increased PONV risk (B1).9 Avoiding intraoperative hypotension (B1)10 and goal directed hemodynamic management (A1)11 may reduce the risk of PONV. Kim et al found that propensity matching, overweight and obese patients [body mass index (BMI) > 25 kg/m2 and > 30 kg/m2 respectively] had significantly lower incidence of PONV than patients with lower BMI (B1).12 Type of Surgery Patients undergoing bariatric surgery have higher rates of PONV (B1).13 Other higher risk surgeries include laparoscopic cholecystectomy, urological procedures, and knee arthroplasty (B1).14 Breast, gynecologic and obstetric surgeries are also associated with increased risk.15 At the population level, adding more risk factors to the prediction model is unlikely to improve model performance. Additional factors should be considered on a case-by-case basis if vomiting poses a significant medical risk, such as an increased intracranial pressure or in conjunction with wired jaws in the postoperative phase. PDNV Risk Evaluation PDNV presents a significant risk as patients no longer have access to fast-onset intravenous (IV) antiemetics or direct care. A simplified PDNV score included 5 risk factors: female gender, age <50 years, history of PONV, opioid use in the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU), and nausea in the PACU (Figure 1B),1 the incidence of PDNV with 0 to 5 risk factors to be about 10%, 20%, 30%, 50%, 60%, and 80%, respectively. Other risk factors may include previous PDNV, length of surgery, antiemetic use in the PACU and postdischarge pain.1 Genomics, Genetics, and Polymorphism Emerging evidence suggests that PONV risk and antiemetics efficacy may be influenced by genetic polymorphisms and variation in gene expression (epigenetics). This includes genetic determinants of cytochrome P450 (CYP 2D6), serotonin, dopamine and acetylcholine receptor activities (SDC 3, Table S2, https://links.lww.com/AA/F570).16 It is however unclear how this may influence PONV risk stratification in the future.17 The Impact of Sex/Race/Gender/Social Determinants on PONV Social determinants, such as sex, gender, race, and socioeconomic status may lead to disparities in health care access, treatment, and outcomes but are infrequently considered in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) related to PONV management.18 Patients with lower socioeconomic status are less likely to receive antiemetics after correcting for potential confounders. The interaction between race/ethnicity and PONV risk is a topic of ongoing debate. It has been observed that African American patients are more frequently undertreated when compared to white patients.19 High-risk Hispanic patients were more likely to experience PONV than white patients.19 Racial disparity in PONV management can be avoided through standardization of care. Sex and gender may impact the perioperative management of PONV, and transgender patients represent a potentially vulnerable population. Transgender patients undergoing facial gender affirming surgery (GAS) were found to have significantly higher risk of PONV than cisgender patients undergoing oral and maxillofacial surgery.20 Gravid women who underwent non-obstetric procedures with general anesthesia have comparable PONV incidence compared to non-gravid patients.21 Fewer prophylactic antiemetics were given among gravid patients, which may be related to the lack of specific recommendations for PONV prophylaxis during pregnancy. GUIDELINE 2. REDUCE BASELINE RISK FOR PONV Approaches for decreasing baseline risk are summarized in SDC 3, Table S3, https://links.lww.com/AA/F570. Propofol Total Intravenous Anesthesia Propofol total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) alone has comparable PONV risk to volatile anesthesia plus 5-hydroxytryptamine 3 (5-HT3) receptor antagonists or droperidol (A1). Both propofol TIVA and subhypnotic dose propofol infusion are effective in combination with other antiemetics (A2).1 Multimodal Systemic Analgesia Effective analgesic interventions for minimizing PONV risk include acetaminophen (A1), intraoperative ketamine (A1), and esmolol infusion (A2). Lidocaine infusion can reduce PONV risk in laparoscopic abdominal procedures, but not in other surgery types (A1).1 Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors (A1) are also effective for reducing PONV risk. titulo: Ethics in hepatology: A professional and very personal journey
resumen: Doing what is the right thing for the individual human being and society….INTRODUCTION When in the 1990s, my former mentor, the late Professor Dame Sheila Sherlock (1918–2001), moderated a clinical case conference, the meeting auditorium was packed with attendees. But however strongly she urged them to stay for the next session on ethical issues in liver transplantation, which she considered would be one of our key challenges in the future, most of the audience walked out. In this context, recent attempts to introduce ethical presentations and topics at meetings of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) were not too successful either. Is this behavior an accurate reflection of hepatologists’ interest in ethics? I hope not. An explicit and specific answer to this question may be lacking, but implicitly ethical issues are prevalent everywhere. The spectrum is broad: ethics involved in coping with life, death, and dying are immediately apparent, but conflicts of interest (COIs), equitable access to care, disparity in health care, integrity in clinical trials, informed consent, ethical business practices, and the duty of the individual to keep silent or to speak up have increasingly come to the forefront in today’s medical world, and the practice of hepatology is no exception. The series editor wants his author(s) to focus mostly on the history of this provocative subject, illuminate, entertain, and amuse but not trivialize, and add to readers’ understanding—all conducted from a personal perspective. As a background to address his charge, we must, of course, start with basic historical principles and then address selected issues that the author deems currently to be of major relevance. EVOLUTION OF HISTORICAL ETHICAL PRINCIPLES AND VIRTUES The principles of medical ethics and their virtues that have been defined and taught to most of us during our student days at medical school represent an evolution since the School of Hippocrates (460–350 bc) (Figure 1). Along the way, they were modified by Jewish, Christian, Muslim, and other teachings, including other possible influences from Hinduism, Buddhism, humanism, and Western philosophy.1–3 When we discuss medical morality and medical ethics, what we are really referring to is our core belief of what is the right medical action and what is the wrong medical action; in essence, the code by which we practice.2FIGURE 1: Major ethical principles and virtues in medicine. Major issue during recent COVID epidemic.The core values codified in current medical ethics include: Autonomy—the right to refuse or choose treatment (Voluntas aegroti suprema lex); Beneficence—the need to act in the best interest of the patient (Salus aegroti suprema lex); Non-maleficence—“First, do no harm” (primum non nocere); Justice—the burden and the benefit of new treatment must be distributed equally; and Respect for persons—the patient has the right to be treated with dignity and honesty. The first agreed code of Christian medical ethics was the 5th century (CE) Formula Comitis Archiatrorum which is credited to a certain Flavius Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus (born c. 484–490 and died c. 577–590 ce). Cassiodorus was a statesman and writer serving in the administration of Theodoric the Great, King of the Ostrogoths—who were members of a division of the Goths, best known for their part in the conquest of Rome in 493 ce shortly after the Roman Empire fell. The Goths were Germanic people likely having arisen from Scandinavia, of whom especially extraordinary was Cassiodorus’s boss, about whom reams have been written.4 Theodoric (454–526 ce), ruler of the combined Gothic realms and an empire stretching from the Atlantic Ocean to the Adriatic Sea, was considered by some to have been a “Western Roman Emperor” in all but name since he ruled a large part of the former Western Roman Empire. Theodoric’s building of churches, palaces, and civic entities like baths, roads, aqueducts, and the like was prodigious. His religion was Arian Christian (nontrinitarian) and though initially tolerant of Catholics, he later showed anger toward them because of Justinian’s ill-treatment of Arian Christians in Constantinople, where he lived as a child. According to John Julius Norwich (1929–2018), the noted British historian and expert on Byzantium, no other Germanic ruler setting up his throne on the ruins of the (western) Roman Empire possessed a fraction of his statesmanship and political vision and when he died, Italy lost the greatest of her early medieval rulers, unparalleled until the days of Charlemagne. Theodoric was undoubtedly a cruel belligerent militarist of his times but may have had a more benign approach toward the common people whom he ruled, but perhaps less so for the Romans than his Goths. As conqueror of Italy, he renewed the ancient Roman institution of Comes Archiatrorum, the court of the chief physicians, and was behind the wording of the oath for those to swear who were appointed to that position. The oath, Formula comitis archiatrorum, is considered the earliest known code of medical ethics that asserted that Medicine should be defined by experienced physicians (and not ephemeral case-based opinions), who should have leisure time to read books within and outside of medicine, and rather than quarrel, which injures patients, they should diligently seek other physicians’ advice about what cures the sick and strengthens the weak. It is debated, however, whether the Formula had an impact on Hippocrates’s stance toward ethics nor the power of Conduct of a physician, the first medical ethics book in Arabic medicine by 9th-century author Ishaq ibn Ali al-Ruhawi’a (إسحاق بن علي الرهاوي), whose Ethics of the Physician contains the first documented description for peer review processes.5 Here it is rewarding to consider the Physicians’ and Pharmacists’ Oath attributed to rabbi, philosopher, and physician Moshe ben Maimon (1135–1204 ce, best known as Maimonides),6 but likely the work of Berlin German-Jewish physician, Marcus Hertz (1747–1803), partly reproduced here: “May I never see in the patient anything but a fellow creature in pain. Grant me the strength, time and opportunity always to correct what I have acquired, always to extend its domain. For knowledge is immense and the spirit of man can extend indefinitely to enrich itself daily with new requirements” Other noteworthy medical ethicists were the 13th century Italian Dominican Frier and priest Thomas Aquinas, and, separated by ~500 hundred years, the English physician Thomas Percival (1740–1804), who published his Medical Ethics in 1803.7 This has since been the dominant influence in Anglo-American medical ethics, and the paradigmatic source for the first and subsequent American Medical Association code that first appeared in 1847,8 in the footprints of the UK Code of Ethics. Medical ethics and jurisprudence (1794, 1803).9 Percival’s Ethics has been criticized as being merely etiquette and not ethics, lacking philosophical substance and perpetuating a spirit of paternalistic condescension unsuited to our democratic times, but these criticisms have been roundly dismissed. Among the most significant medical ethical judgments, so to speak came in 1948 from the Nuremberg10,11 trials that singularly included the “Doctors Trial,” addressing medical atrocities during World War II, such as euthanizing persons unworthy of life (mentally ill and disabled) and perpetrating horrible experiments including infecting prisoners with agents believed to cause epidemic jaundice, from which the German Army, and obviously other armies, were supposed to benefit. The accused included in their defense that they had been adhering to research methodology taught to them in the United States. The court handed out major sentences (death by hanging and years of imprisonment) and proposed rules (the Nuremberg Code, which is reproduced in a reference cited here12) that brought informed consent to the forefront of biomedical research. We can interject here for its hepatological relevance, the case of Hans Eppinger,12 one of the most revered (and truthfully feared) hepatologists of his day, physician to the famous, especially in Europe (such as the Queen of Romania, Stalin, and others). Eppinger had recognized the significance of spider nevi before William Bennet Bean13 and spurned the theory of catarrhal jaundice before Dame Sheila disproved it.14 Eppinger committed suicide when summoned to give evidence in Nuremberg. titulo: “We Had A Symbiotic Relationship”: The Structure and Texture of Chinese-White Relationships in Depression-Era Utah
resumen: Utah in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries was an international, multiethnic space. Latter-day Saint converts from Scandinavia, the British Isles, Germany, and other places in Europe streamed in via the transcontinental railroad to practice their religion together. Railroad and mine workers came via those same transportation networks from southern Europe, eastern Europe, and Asia.1 Chinese had been a presence in the American West since the Gold Rush and the era of railroad building. For decades, they filled niches in Utah's economy, including railroad construction, mining, vegetable farming, and the restaurant and laundry business.2Strikingly, the missionary-minded Latter-day Saints, who had sent evangelists to Hong Kong in 1853, to New Zealand in the 1880s, and who had even built a temple in Laie, Hawaii, in 1919, to accommodate the spiritual needs of a burgeoning community of Hawaiian members, appear to have made almost no sustained efforts to proselytize to the non-Christian Chinese in their midst in Utah.3This was not for lack of regular interactions between non-Christian Chinese and White Latter-day Saints. For example, in 1917, Chinese-owned laundries were a common enough feature of everyday life in Utah that a writer for the Relief Society Magazine suggested a “Chinese laundry”-themed moneymaking booth, a spin on the fishpond, at bazaars and fairs. “Tickets at 10c or 5c are sold by a ‘Chinaman,’ who circulates among the people. If the right one is chosen for this job he will be very popular with the little folks.”4 From the “Chinese laundry” booth, children presented their tickets and received prize packages wrapped up as laundry bundles. The role of the “Chinaman” clearly involved some sort of cross-racial costuming, and was a comical, buffoonish role in which the humor relied on people's familiarity with the roles Chinese played in their communities, albeit in a stereotypical and shallow way. The White Latter-day Saints’ focus on the laundry (a place of business) in association with people of Chinese ethnicity suggests that the relationship between the two groups was most frequently defined through economic, not fraternal or ecclesiastical, interactions.Because of social separations between non-Christian Chinese and White Latter-day Saint populations, historical understanding of interactions between these two groups before the post-World War II era is very sparse. We seek to shed more light on these interactions at the grassroots by telling the story of a neighborly friendship between two families, the Jus and the Soderborgs, in Depression-era Utah. This story is unusual for two reasons. First, there is a dearth of primary sources on Chinese nuclear families in Utah at this time, with most of the sources focusing on bachelor male sojourners. Second, the reciprocal and neighborly relationship between the two families counters the broader systematic racial hierarchies and segregations within Utah society and within church culture at the time. Encountering each other at a liminal moment in their lives in Depression-era Utah, the Jus and Soderborgs became part of each other's lives in intimate, symbiotic ways, including religious exchanges, that defied the larger forces of anti-Chinese racism and segregation within Latter-day Saint communities.Our positionality as historians trying to illuminate this aspect of Utah history is quite unique. We are the second- and third-generation descendants of members of the White and Chinese families we describe. The bulk of our sources are oral histories from senior family members. We were both working as historians on other topics, but ran into each other at a Mormon History Association meeting in 2021 and decided to write a paper together on our joint family histories. We believe that the significance of this research goes far beyond our individual family heritage, however, because of the overall lack of primary sources on Chinese families in Utah society and a corresponding lack of primary sources on interethnic and interreligious relations between Chinese practicing traditional ancestral worship religion and White Latter-day Saints.Probably one reason for the lack of programmatic proselytization of Utah-based Chinese on the same level as a Latter-day Saint international mission is the specter of racial integration. For a White missionary, it was one thing to convert Māori in New Zealand or Hawaiians in Hawaii, but another thing entirely to practice religion with them in integrated congregations in one's own neighborhood. In marked contrast with their policy toward White European, Australian, and New Zealand converts, Church leaders encouraged non-White converts from New Zealand and the Pacific Islands to remain in their homelands instead of emigrating to Utah. When the desire of Pacific Islanders to experience ordinances within the sacred space of a Latter-day Saint temple became so great that many Pacific Islanders did emigrate to Utah in the 1880s, Latter-day Saint leaders arranged for them to be segregated in their own settlement in Skull Valley over sixty miles from the White Latter-day Saint population in Salt Lake City.5This general racism within Latter-day Saint communities in Utah was part of larger forces of racial discrimination enshrined in the laws of the United States. The Chinese Exclusion Act, passed by the U.S. Congress in 1882, effectively banned the immigration of Chinese men, but even earlier, beginning in 1870, Chinese women were banned. All Chinese women coming to the United States were labeled “prostitutes,” which made them inadmissible.6 Another law that stigmatized Chinese and restricted their life choices was the Utah law against intermarriage between Whites and Blacks and between Whites and Asians, in force from 1888 to 1963. In 1922, Congress passed the Cable Act, which decreed that White women who married Asian men would lose their U.S. citizenship.7 One consequence of this pattern of discriminatory laws is that the Chinese in Utah were overwhelmingly male bachelors. There were very few Chinese families with a father, mother, and children.8Table 1 shows the ratio of men to women in the federal censuses from 1860 to 1940 (except 1900).In addition to exclusionary immigration laws, Chinese already living in Utah experienced persistent prejudice and discrimination. The largest community of ethnic Chinese in Utah was concentrated around Plum Alley in downtown Salt Lake City. They were largely confined by social pressures to the cramped, squalid, poorly maintained streets and living quarters of Salt Lake City's Chinatown. When they tried to venture outside this cordon without fitting into the role of those Chinese “allowed” to be outside, they were often harassed or attacked. Historian Michael Lansing notes that within Salt Lake City, random violence such as beatings or rock-throwing against Chinese was much more likely outside Chinatown than within it.9Beyond violence, harassment was often leveled at Chinese outside of Chinatown in the form of legal actions or fines for petty offenses to which White members of the population were rarely subjected. Sometimes, they arrested them just for being in neighborhoods where it looked like they didn't “belong.” Lansing writes that in September 1898, a Chinese man named Chung Chung was arrested and brought in to police court because he had been “hanging around a residence on the West Side.”10 Chung Chung explained that he had been looking for work at the garden of a fellow Chinese and had gotten lost. In the same month, a policeman fined Ching Ying $2 for violating the bicycle ordinance. This ordinance required all bicycles in use in the city limits to have a bell and a light and was rarely enforced.11 White citizens, including police, tended to see Chinese outside of Plum Alley as suspect.Chinese in Utah also experienced racial discrimination in the form of restricted access to private and public spaces. Real estate restrictions and community covenants barred non-White people from purchasing property.12 Beginning in the World War II era, fueled by racial hatred of the Japanese, the Utah state legislature codified a law banning Asians from property ownership. Even before this, informal norms restricted Chinese opportunities to rent or own property. With regard to access to space more generally, Chinese were excluded from public recreation facilities along with other non-White persons. Helen Gim Kurumada, who grew up in Salt Lake City in the 1940s, recalled, “Discrimination was absolutely public in Salt Lake. We couldn't go to city swimming pools. . . . When we went to a movie at one of the better theaters, we couldn't sit downstairs. We had to go . . . to the balconies.”13In sum, Chinese Americans in Utah lived amidst formal and informal structures of racism that constrained their opportunities for socialization, marriage and family, property ownership, and even just being present in a space.But racism and isolation were not the only reality of the lives of Chinese in Utah. They demonstrated extraordinary resilience both in their presence as fixtures within the community and in their determination to pursue their own personal goals. The scant sources we have, though imperfect, capture glimpses of the vital niche Chinese enterprises filled in Utah's economy, normal human-to-human interactions that were not dominated by overwhelming racism, and evidence of reciprocity between the Latter-day Saints and their Chinese neighbors.Perhaps the most significant exception to these spatial segregations were Chinese gardeners. They did live outside the city center, in farming plots interspersed throughout more suburban and rural neighborhoods. Insulated from their neighbors by open space, they could largely keep to themselves.Walter Jones has done considerable work tracking the success of Chinese vegetable gardeners in Utah from the 1860s to 1911. His work details how, as the “agrarian ideal” of the early Mormon settlers began to give way to urbanization and industrialization, Chinese vegetable gardeners succeeded in locating plots of abandoned land and turning them into productive small farms.14 Latter-day Saint negative attitudes toward Chinese were tempered by Latter-day Saint admiration for the farmers’ work ethic and agrarian occupation at a time when agriculture was going out of style in Salt Lake City.15 Because they were always outside, working, visible to all, Chinese farmers were a literal part of the Utah landscape. Their farms were local landmarks. Small-scale farmers sold their produce door to door, directly interacting with housewives.16One of the rare Chinese families who made a living as truck farmers in Depression-era Salt Lake City was the Ju family. It began in 1919 when a nineteen-year-old named Ju Gin Gor (周公珍, 1900–2003), also known as Ju Gin, came to America as a “paper son” (relying on false immigration documents in which his uncle in Utah claimed him as his own son). Ju Gin grew up in a farming village in Kaiping, China. In this area of the southeastern province of Guangdong, many “castle houses” were built by sojourners who had gone overseas to work and came back wealthy. His uncle, Ju Joy, was a well-to-do merchant who had already established himself in Utah. On the immigration papers, to fit the profile of one of Ju Joy's sons, Ju Gin listed his age as younger than he actually was.At first, Ju Gin worked in Park City as a cook in a mining camp, one of the “acceptable” occupations for Chinese. But he soon struck out on his own. His only assets were relatives, some savings, and unquenchable confidence in his own ability. He chose farming, a vocation he knew well, in an industry where he could thrive without threatening the livelihood of white people. He was willing to work hard and he had some good fortune to make a few friends in his community.
